lessons.title: Graph Traversal Overview
lessons.concept: Graph traversal means visiting nodes/vertices of a graph in a systematic way. The two fundamental traversals are Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS). Traversals are used for searching, connectivity checks, path finding (unweighted for BFS shortest path in edges), and many graph algorithms. A visited set/array is needed to avoid revisiting nodes in graphs with cycles.
lessons.formula: Maintain visited to prevent infinite loops in cyclic graphs. Time depends on representation: O(V+E) with adjacency list for BFS/DFS.
lessons.worked_example: In a connected undirected graph, starting BFS/DFS from one node with visited tracking will reach all nodes; in a disconnected graph, repeat from unvisited nodes to cover all components.
mistakes: Forgetting visited tracking in cyclic/undirected graphs
Confusing graph traversal with tree traversal where no cycles exist
Not handling disconnected graphs when full coverage is required

lessons.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
lessons.concept: BFS explores neighbors level by level from a starting node using a queue (FIFO). It first visits all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, etc. In an unweighted graph, BFS finds the shortest path in terms of number of edges from the source to reachable nodes.
lessons.formula: BFS: enqueue start, mark visited; while queue not empty: u=dequeue, process u, for each unvisited neighbor v enqueue and mark visited. Uses queue.
lessons.worked_example: Graph edges 1-2,1-3,2-4 from source 1: BFS order can be 1,2,3,4 (level 0:1, level 1:2,3, level 2:4).
mistakes: Using a stack instead of a queue for BFS
Marking visited when dequeued instead of when enqueued (can cause duplicates in queue)
Assuming BFS gives shortest path in weighted graphs without modification
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
lessons.concept: DFS explores as far as possible along one branch before backtracking. It can be implemented recursively (using call stack) or iteratively using an explicit stack. DFS is useful for cycle detection, topological sorting (on DAGs), connectivity, and exploring components.
lessons.formula: DFS: visit node, mark visited, recursively/stack-visit each unvisited neighbor. Uses stack/recursion (LIFO behavior).
lessons.worked_example: Same graph from source 1: DFS order could be 1,2,4,3 (go deep via 2 to 4, backtrack to visit 3) depending on neighbor order.
mistakes: Assuming DFS traversal order is unique without specifying neighbor order
Stack overflow risk for very deep recursion in some environments
Confusing DFS with BFS level-order behavior

practice.explanation: Because BFS explores in increasing order of edge distance from the source, it yields shortest paths (fewest edges) in unweighted graphs.

practice.question: Why is a visited structure important in graph traversal?

options.B: To avoid revisiting nodes and infinite loops in cyclic graphs

practice.explanation: Graphs can contain cycles; tracking visited nodes prevents repeated processing and non-terminating traversal.

practice.question: Time complexity of BFS/DFS using adjacency list representation is:
practice.explanation: Each vertex is visited once and each edge is explored (once or twice depending on directed/undirected), giving O(V+E).
